content:
The Probability chapter is a high-yield part of the CAT Quantitative Aptitude section, and a favourite in XAT, SNAP, NMAT and CMAT too. This guide explains what CAT Probability tests, the formulas and shortcuts worth memorising, the mistakes that cost marks, and a free 10-question online test you can take right now.

Take the quiz below first, read the explanation for anything you miss, then use the chapter e-book at the end for full, exam-level practice.

What CAT asks on Probability

Classical probability, the addition rule, independent and mutually exclusive events, and conditional probability.

Key formulas & shortcuts

  • P(E) = favourable/total, 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1; P(not E) = 1 − P(E).
  • P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B).
  • Independent: P(A∩B) = P(A)·P(B).
  • Conditional: P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B).

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Adding probabilities of non-mutually-exclusive events without subtracting the overlap.
  • Confusing independent with mutually exclusive events.
  • Miscounting the sample space.

questions.q: A die is thrown three times. A: 4 on the third throw; B: 6 on the first and 5 on the second throw. Then P(Amid B) is

faq.q: Are mutually exclusive and independent the same?
faq.a: No. Mutually exclusive means they can’t both happen (P(A∩B)=0); independent means one doesn’t affect the other (P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)).
P(not E) = 1 − P(E) — often the fastest route for "at least one" questions.
